stem:
A clinically stable patient is being followed by an early pregnancy service after ultrasound showed neither an intrauterine nor an ectopic pregnancy. Serum hCG rises from 600 to 1,200 IU/L over 48 hours (non-pregnant reference <5 IU/L). She remains pain-free and asks whether the result proves that the pregnancy is in the uterus.

Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: A normal rise makes an ectopic unlikely enough to discharge her
options.explanation: Some ectopic pregnancies show a rise like this, so a normal-looking rise does not allow discharge from follow-up.

options.label: B
options.text: Above 1,000 IU/L, an empty uterus on scan now means an ectopic
options.explanation: No single hCG level, including 1,000 IU/L, makes an empty uterus diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy; a viable intrauterine pregnancy may still be too early to see.

options.label: C
options.text: hCG cannot show location; she needs further ultrasound follow-up
options.explanation: A pregnancy of unknown location stays unknown until ultrasound shows where it is. The rise suggests ongoing trophoblast but cannot place it, so she continues follow-up with a repeat scan.

options.label: D
options.text: The rise shows an intrauterine pregnancy that is too small to see
options.explanation: A rise is consistent with an early intrauterine pregnancy, but ectopic pregnancies can rise similarly, so it does not establish location.

options.label: E
options.text: The rise excludes a failing pregnancy, leaving only location unknown
options.explanation: A rising level does not rule out a pregnancy that will fail, and it does not settle location.

context: A rising hCG cannot show where a pregnancy is; location of a pregnancy of unknown location is established by ultrasound.
